children: Apollo Global Management Chief Executive Marc Rowan said on Wednesday that energy infrastructure and transition including artificial intelligence and data centers are the drivers of his company's business.

In an interview at the Dow Jones Energy Forum in New York, Rowan said the main driving force of Apollo, a global alternative asset manager that oversees $1 trillion in assets, is not the company's well-known private-equity business.

Instead, he said the driver of Apollo's business today includes energy pipelines, energy transmission, energy transition, next-gen manufacturing, defense, infrastructure as well as AI and the data center industry.
"Energy is a big part of it because energy is the underpinning of AI and data.
Energy is the underpinning of industrialization, re-industrialization. Energy is the underpinning of movement to EV," Rowan said.
In addition, Rowan said Apollo will provide a "very large percentage" - between $50 billion and $75 billion - of its loan origination this year to the energy and AI companies.

Rowan said a main goal of the prominent private-equity firm is providing loans for what he called "very long-dated" investments in infrastructure needed to transport energy in various forms including those in the U.S., Canada, the Middle East and Europe.

"It's very clear that the driver of this is demand for energy, demand for electricity. You cannot be AI-sovereign without models, chips and energy. And that's where we are and almost everyone is short energy," he said.
Asked how much of Apollo's financing will go to the energy sector, Rowan said "a very large percentage. ... But of the $400-$500 billion we will originate this year, it'll be $50-75 billion."

In 2025, Apollo originated about $309 billion of assets. Private-equity firms or hedge funds act as a direct lender to issue debt to a borrower in return for upfront origination fees and interest on the loan.
Rowan also said that the U.S. has sharply lagged China in terms of growing power-generation capacity to meet the future demand of data centers.
"We (U.S.) went through a period where we were uber-focused on decarbonization and the source of energy as opposed to the transition to lower-intensity forms of energy," Rowan said.

"And what's really catapulted this is the whole AI data center revolution. The numbers for the U.S. for AI and data ... essentially encompassed the totality of all of the energy that exists," he added.

The data centers that power AI use a large amount of electricity and can stretch thin the power grid. In June, Chevron and Microsoft signed a 20-year power supply agreement to develop a power facility in West Texas near Chevron's natural gas-production sites.

In 1990, Rowan co-founded Apollo with other hedge fund pioneers including Leon Black. Apollo has been known for its private-equity and distressed buyouts as well as massive credit and retirement services.
